z.f: Receive and launch daily essentials
z.i: keys, wallet, sunglasses, phone, mail, handbag, backpack, work badge
z.s: small tray, mail sorter, labeled hooks, charging dock
z.g: A clear arrival surface with only current-day essentials in defined homes and no loose paper
z.h: blocked exit path, trip hazards, overloaded outlets
z.c: Place the tray where your hand naturally lands on entry — moving a key bowl 30 cm from the natural drop point is the difference between a system and a suggestion.

call.x: What you have been avoiding here is not the keys, it is the six sheets of paper you keep shifting from one end of the surface to the other. They stay because each needs a small unpleasant action: a form, a phone call, a payment. The rule is that nothing returns to the surface without a verdict, and there are only three: act, file, recycle. If it is act, it stands upright in the folder with the date written in the corner. When any item in that folder passes fourteen days, it stops being paperwork and becomes a decision. Do it tonight, or accept honestly that you never will and recycle it. Both of those are answers. Leaving it on the surface is not.

z.f: Store frequently used outerwear
z.i: coats, jackets, hats, scarves, gloves, umbrellas
z.s: hooks, hangers, upper shelf bins, umbrella stand
z.g: Current-season outerwear is easy to retrieve and return, with off-season items relocated
z.c: Hooks beat hangers for daily outerwear by a factor of ten in compliance; save hangers for the closet and occasion coats.

call.t: The coat you feel guilty about
call.x: Somewhere on this rail is a good coat that cost real money and goes outside roughly never. It survives every clear-out because getting rid of it feels like admitting to the money. The rule is that coats are counted by weather, not by number. Each person gets one coat per kind of weather your climate genuinely produces: wet, cold, and something in between. A second coat in the same category has to beat the first one on a specific, nameable day. If you cannot name that day, that is the coat that leaves. The expensive one is not exempt, because the money is already spent whether it hangs here or keeps someone else warm. Give it one trial: front hook, most reachable spot, two weeks. If you did not reach for it, you have your answer and you had it before you started.

z.f: Contain footwear used near the entrance
z.i: daily shoes, boots, slippers, shoe-care supplies
z.s: shoe rack, boot tray, labeled basket
z.g: Only current footwear remains, pairs are visible, and the walking path is clear
z.h: trip hazards, wet footwear, blocked door
z.c: Store soles-down on trays, current season only; a two-pairs-per-person cap at the door keeps the zone self-limiting.

call.t: The worn out pair you keep for the garden
call.x: Everyone has a pair with the tread rubbed smooth that survives on the grounds that it is fine for mucky jobs. Count them honestly and there are usually three such pairs and about one muddy job a year. The rule is that the sole decides, not the memory. Turn the shoe over. If the tread has gone smooth or the heel has worn through on the outer edge, that shoe is no longer safe on a wet step or a slick pavement, which means it is not gardening footwear, it is rubbish with sentimental value attached. Keep exactly one dirty-job pair per person and store it where the dirty jobs happen, not at the front door. The pair you would be embarrassed to be seen in is not a spare. It is a decision you already made and have not carried out.

z.f: Support short transition tasks
z.i: mail, decor, bags, pet items, small tools, seasonal accessories
z.s: shallow drawer dividers, baskets, tray
z.g: The surface supports one clear purpose and the interior storage is categorized
z.c: Keep the surface standard to three items or fewer — flat surfaces near doors are clutter magnets with a 24-hour relapse rate.

call.x: This drawer becomes the second junk drawer within a month of being emptied. It happens every time, because it is the nearest place to set down something you do not want to carry any further. The decision being avoided is not what to throw away. It is admitting the drawer needs a job at all. The rule: this drawer serves the door and nothing else. One test question per item, would you need this while wearing your shoes, either on the way out or in the first ten seconds back in. Dog lead, yes. Sun cream, yes. Spare car charger, yes. The screwdriver, the birthday candles and the case for a phone you no longer own all fail, and they fail even though they genuinely have nowhere better to live. Find them somewhere better today, in another room, with a name on it. If you do not, they will be back in this drawer by the weekend and so will four of their friends.

z.f: Provide a clean and safe threshold
z.i: door hardware, doormat, floor mat, shoe debris, pet hair
z.s: defined mat boundary and no-storage floor rule
z.g: The threshold is clean, unobstructed, functional, and ready for safe entry and exit
z.c: Two-mat systems (coarse outside, absorbent inside) capture the majority of tracked-in soil before it reaches the first rug.

call.x: A mat looks perfectly fine long after it has stopped working, and the decision being dodged is spending money to replace something that is not visibly broken. So test it instead of looking at it. Walk in from outside on a dry gritty day, wipe your feet the way you actually wipe them, then lift the mat and look at both the floor beneath it and the fibres themselves. A working mat holds grit down inside its pile and drops a clear line of dirt when you shake it out. A finished mat has fibres flattened all in one direction, and the grit sits on top of them and walks straight off on the next pair of shoes. If it fails that test, replace it this month rather than next winter. A worn mat is not saving you anything. It is quietly sanding the finish off every floor between this door and the kitchen.

z.f: Prepare food on an open work surface
z.i: cutting boards, knives, mixing bowls, small appliances, oils, utensils
z.s: counter boundary, knife storage, appliance homes
z.g: A mostly open counter with only active daily-prep tools and at least one full clear work area
z.h: knife exposure, hot appliance clearance, cord hazards
z.c: Clear counter is production capacity: a 60 cm clear run of workspace is the minimum viable prep zone — protect it like a fire lane.

call.x: The hard one is the appliance you genuinely love and rarely use: the mixer, the bread machine, the espresso setup. Count real uses over the past month, not the ones you intended. Anything you reach for less than a couple of times a week comes off the counter and goes to a low cabinet, ideally on a pull-out. Anything you have not switched on in a year leaves the kitchen entirely. And if your honest reason for keeping it out is that lifting it from a cabinet would stop you using it, you have just proved the machine is not part of your cooking, and it is worth more sold than stored.

z.f: Cook at the range, oven, or cooktop
z.i: pots, pans, utensils, spices, oils, pot holders, timers
z.s: utensil crock, drawer dividers, spice rack, pan storage
z.g: Frequently used cooking tools are within safe reach and the cooktop area is clear
z.c: Store by reach-while-cooking: oils, salt, and the three most-used utensils within one step of the burners; everything else is a drawer item.

call.t: The spice rack you are not honest about
call.x: Every cook keeps jars bought for one recipe from one holiday. Open them and smell them, one by one, over the bin. Ground spices fade first, and if a jar smells of dust rather than of itself, it is no longer seasoning anything you cook, and keeping it does not recover what you paid. Then make the harder call underneath: keep spices for the food you cooked in the last year, not the food you imagine cooking. If you want that cuisine back, buy the two spices fresh on the day you cook it. A rack you can read is worth more than a rack that is complete.

z.f: Wash food, dishes, and hands
z.i: dish soap, brushes, sponges, drying rack, dishwasher supplies
z.s: sink caddy, under-sink tray, drying boundary
z.g: The sink is empty, clean, and ready; cleaning tools are sanitary and contained
z.c: An empty sink at day's end is the kitchen's keystone habit — it resets the whole room's standard while the coffee brews.

call.x: The real decision in this zone is not what to keep, it is whether you let the basin be a staging area. Soaking is the word a kitchen uses for postponing, and one soaking pan gives every other dish permission to join it. Settle it with a deadline rather than a ban: a pan may soak, but only until the current dishwasher cycle ends or until you next leave the room, whichever comes first. If a dish cannot meet that deadline, it gets washed now or goes in the machine dirty. The rule holds because it names a moment, and moments arrive on their own.

z.f: Store daily dishes and light serving items
z.i: plates, bowls, cups, glasses, mugs, serving ware
z.s: shelf risers, category shelves, labels
z.g: Daily-use items are grouped, reachable, and retrievable without moving unrelated items
z.c: Eye-level shelves are prime real estate: daily dishes there, occasional items above, and nothing you'd need a chair for more than monthly.

call.x: Almost every kitchen holds two sets: the one you eat off and the good one, or the one from before you moved. Pick one everyday set, sized to the people who eat here plus two, and give it the shelf between shoulder and eye height. Then decide the second set honestly. If it has not been on a table in two years and nobody has asked to inherit it, it goes now, whole, to somewhere it will be used. If it is genuinely somebody's grandmother's, sentiment gets to keep the objects but does not get to keep the shelf you reach into daily: box it, label it, and store it outside the kitchen. What you cannot do is keep both sets at eye level and then blame the cabinet for being full.

z.f: Store heavy cookware and larger kitchen tools
z.i: pots, pans, lids, bakeware, colanders, mixing bowls
z.s: lid rack, pull-out shelves, pan dividers
z.g: Cookware is nested or separated, lids are contained, and heavy items are stored low
z.c: Nest by size with lid organizers vertical; if a pot hasn't cooked in a year, it's donation inventory occupying your best low storage.

call.x: Cook a normal week and count the most pans you had going at once. That number plus one is your cap, and everything beyond it goes, including the expensive one you never liked using. The money is already spent, and keeping the pan does not get any of it back; it only costs you the low shelf. Then handle the guest argument separately: if a piece earns its place twice a year for visitors, and a roasting tray you already own could do the same job, keep the tray and release the piece. A cookware set kept for a hypothetical dinner party takes up the easiest shelf in the kitchen every day of the year for two evenings of use.

z.f: Store hand tools used for cooking and serving
z.i: flatware, spatulas, peelers, measuring tools, foil, wraps, towels
z.s: drawer dividers, labels, quantity limits
z.g: Each drawer has one clear category and every tool fits within its divider
z.c: Dividers first, then a hard rule: one of each tool unless you genuinely cook with two. Duplicate spatulas are how drawers die.

call.t: The drawer everyone calls the junk drawer
call.x: A kitchen is allowed one drawer of small useful things, but it has to be a named drawer with a category and a divider, not an amnesty. Write its list: tape, string, a torch, batteries, a working pen, the takeaway menus you actually order from. Everything in there must be something you would come to the kitchen looking for. Then take an empty box, and anything you cannot name a use for while you are holding it goes in the box. Date the box, put it on a shelf, and if nothing has been pulled out of it by the end of the season it leaves unopened. The screws in the envelope and the manual for the dead printer are not kitchen items, and they are the reason the drawer no longer opens.

z.f: Preserve current food and make inventory visible
z.i: produce, dairy, meat, leftovers, condiments, frozen food, ice
z.s: clear bins, date labels, zones, first-in-first-out
z.g: Food is current, grouped, dated where needed, and visible without overfilling
z.c: Assign shelves by category and temperature — raw proteins low and sealed, leftovers at eye level with dates — and run a weekly eye-level purge before grocery day.

call.t: The container you keep moving to the front
call.x: The genuinely hard call here is not the obviously spoiled food, it is the container of good leftovers you have now shifted forward three times. Ask what would actually have to happen for it to be eaten, and be concrete: which meal, which day, who eats it. If you cannot answer, it is not food you are storing, it is the guilt of having cooked too much. Bin it today, then fix the cause rather than the symptom: cook a smaller batch, or portion leftovers into a lunch container the same evening you cook, before the fridge door closes. A leftover that goes in already assigned to a meal gets eaten. A leftover that goes in undecided is a decision you have only postponed at four degrees.

z.f: Support daily hygiene and grooming
z.i: soap, toothbrushes, skincare, hair tools, cosmetics
z.s: daily tray, toothbrush holder, heat-tool rest
z.g: The counter is mostly clear with only daily-use items in defined positions
z.c: Daily items on one liftable tray, everything else in drawers — the counter should clean in one swipe.

call.x: The straightener or the dryer sits on the counter because the outlet is right there and you use it three or four times a week. That convenience is exactly what is costing you a clear counter, and it is the decision you keep stepping around. The rule that settles it: the counter holds only what you touch every single day. Three times a week is a drawer tool, so buy the heat-safe pouch, give it a drawer, and accept the few seconds it costs you. If the drawer genuinely will not reach from where you stand to dry your hair, the honest fix is a wall-mounted holder beside the mirror, not the counter.

z.f: Store personal-care tools and products
z.i: makeup, razors, combs, brushes, dental supplies
z.s: drawer dividers, category labels, quantity limits
z.g: Products are current, grouped, divided, and visible without digging
z.c: Drawer dividers by routine (morning, evening, weekly) and a hard expiry check every Sort pass — open cosmetics age in months, not years.

call.t: The expensive shade you never wear
call.x: There is a palette or a bottle in there that cost more than you like to remember, and you have used it twice. Keeping it is not thrift, it is paying storage on a decision that already went wrong, and you skip past it on every Sort pass because binning it means admitting the money is gone. The money is gone either way. The rule: if it is open and past its window, or you reached for something else the last three times, it leaves today. If it is unopened and still in date, it gets one season, and you write that season on a strip of tape stuck to the base so the clock is visible instead of imaginary.

z.f: Store cleaning supplies and backstock around plumbing
z.i: cleaners, paper goods, toiletries, plumbing items
z.s: leak tray, slide-out organizers, turntable, labels
z.g: Plumbing remains accessible and supplies are contained in pull-outs or turntables
z.c: Two stacked pull-out bins double usable volume around the P-trap, and a leak-alert mat turns the cabinet floor into an early-warning system.

call.x: You have packed this cabinet wall to wall because it is the only storage in the room, and the P-trap is now buried behind a tower of paper towels. Here is the arithmetic you have been avoiding: a joint that weeps unnoticed for months turns a cheap washer into a rotted cabinet base and a floor that has to come up. The rule: the trap joint and both shut-off valves stay visible whenever the doors are open, and nothing sits on the tray. If that means the backstock will not fit, the backstock leaves this room, not the sightline. Spare shampoo and toilet rolls can live in a linen cupboard. A leak cannot live anywhere else.

z.f: Store medicines and small daily-care items
z.i: OTC medicine, first aid, eye care, prescriptions, grooming items
z.s: shelf labels, dated bins, lockable section
z.g: Only current approved items remain, grouped by purpose and secured as needed
z.c: Medicines actually prefer a cool, dry bedroom shelf over a humid bathroom cabinet; either way, child-secure and expiry-checked twice a year, disposed via take-back.

call.x: There is a half-course of antibiotics in here, or a bottle of strong painkillers from a procedure two years ago, and you keep it because it might come in useful and because handing it back feels like waste. It is the single most common thing in this cabinet that should not be in it. The rule: a medicine belongs to a condition someone in this house has now, prescribed to that person, in date, with the label intact. Everything else goes in the take-back bag today, including the one you are quietly telling yourself is still fine. Leftover painkillers sitting behind a mirror are the most likely thing in this room to seriously hurt a visitor, and nothing about not wasting them outweighs that.

z.f: Support bathing and routine cleaning
z.i: shampoo, conditioner, soap, razors, toys, squeegee
z.s: caddy zones, bottle limit, hooks
z.g: Only active products remain, surfaces are clean, and the floor is slip-resistant
z.c: Spray, then wait: cleaner dwell time does the scrubbing. Squeegee after each use and the weekly clean drops to minutes.

call.t: The bottle you are keeping out of guilt
call.x: There are four or five bottles in there you do not use. Some cost too much to admit, some were gifts, and some hold an inch you cannot bring yourself to pour away. Meanwhile the caddy never dries out, the shelf grows a ring, and you shift eight bottles to clean a space that should hold four. The rule: a product is in use if you touched it in the last two weeks of showers. If you did not, it leaves the enclosure today. The inch in the bottom is not saved money, it is what keeps mold on your shelf, so use it this week or pour it out and recycle the bottle. Gifts get no exemption for being gifts.

z.f: Support sanitation and replenishment
z.i: toilet paper, brush, cleaner, trash can, hygiene supplies
z.s: reserve-roll limit, brush home, lined bin
z.g: The area is clean, minimally stocked, and supplies are contained
z.c: Brush and bowl treatment weekly with full dwell; keep a dedicated cloth color for toilet-only duty and never let it near a counter.

call.t: What you keep within splash range
call.x: The cistern lid is the most tempting shelf in the room, and every flush throws a fine mist across it. The decision you have been avoiding is not whether that is true, it is which of your things you are willing to keep there anyway. Settle it with one line: nothing that touches your face, your mouth, or your food goes within arm's reach of the bowl. Toothbrushes, lens cases, hand cream, drinking glasses, and open candles all move out. What may stay is the brush, the lidded bin, the reserve rolls, and cleaner stored high. If that leaves the lid bare, that is the right answer, and it has the useful side effect that the lid finally gets wiped.

z.f: Store towels, washcloths, and bathroom linens
z.i: bath towels, hand towels, washcloths, mats
z.s: shelf labels, folding standard, set quantities
z.g: Linens are clean, complete, folded by type, and held within capacity
z.c: Three sets per person or bed — one in use, one in wash, one on shelf — folded to a uniform footprint, sets nested in a pillowcase.

call.t: The good towels you never use
call.x: You have a set kept back for guests who visit twice a year, and three thin gray towels you reach for every single day because using the good ones feels like spending them. That is a shelf running backwards, and it has been running backwards for years. The rule: rank every towel you own, use the top of that ranking daily, and let the worn ones go now instead of after another year of being the ones you actually touch. Keep exactly one guest set, in a pillowcase, and put everything else into rotation. A towel saved for a better occasion is a towel wearing out in a cupboard while you dry yourself on a rag.

z.f: Support restorative sleep
z.i: mattress, pillows, sheets, blankets, bedside textiles
z.s: linen set standard, under-bed limits
z.g: The bed is clean, made to a simple standard, and free of stored clutter
z.c: Make the bed to the standard every morning — it's the room's largest visual surface, and it sets the compliance tone for every other zone.

call.x: You are holding four or five sets because one was a wedding gift, one is new but scratchy, and one is the good set you have never slept on. Two per bed is the honest number: one on, one clean. Keep a third only if a child or a pet actually sleeps here and you have stripped this bed at two in the morning within the last year. Anything past three is a set you wash, fold, and never put on a bed. And the good one goes on tonight, because a sheet saved for an occasion is a sheet nobody ever uses.

z.f: Support one sleeper's nighttime routine
z.i: lamp, phone, charger, book, glasses, medication, water
z.s: small tray, cable clip, drawer divider
z.g: Only current nighttime essentials remain and the surface is mostly clear
z.c: Five items or fewer on top; a small drawer tray keeps the inside from becoming the junk drawer's bedroom franchise.

call.x: You know the phone should not sleep here, and you have kept it because it is your alarm. That is one job, and a nine pound clock does it. Buy the clock, move the charger to the dresser across the room, and give the phone a landing spot you have to stand up to reach. If you will not commit to that, then commit to the honest version instead: the charger stays, the phone lies face down, and something else comes off the top so you are still at five. What you cannot keep doing is calling the current arrangement temporary.

z.f: Support one sleeper's nighttime routine
z.i: lamp, phone, charger, book, glasses, medication, water
z.s: small tray, cable clip, drawer divider
z.g: Only current nighttime essentials remain and the surface is mostly clear
z.c: Five items or fewer on top; a small drawer tray keeps the inside from becoming the junk drawer's bedroom franchise.

call.t: Whose things you are allowed to throw away
call.x: You want to fix this side because you can see it from yours, and every argument about tidiness in a shared bedroom starts right here. The rule that settles it: you clean, they cull. You may wipe, vacuum and straighten anything on this side, and you may not remove a single object from it. Finish your own nightstand to the standard, leave theirs untouched, and let the difference between the two tops be the entire argument you make. If they never change a thing, you have still fixed half the room and kept the marriage. The one item you can raise out loud is the out of date medication, because that is a safety question and not a taste question.

z.f: Support limited daily dressing or display
z.i: jewelry, fragrance, decor, pocket contents, folded clothes
z.s: valet tray, jewelry organizer, display boundary
z.g: The top has one defined landing tray and no clothing backlog
z.c: A single tray or valet for daily-carry items; the dresser top is the bedroom's landing zone and needs the same cap.

call.x: There are three or four bottles standing up here and you wear one of them. The others were gifts, or they were expensive, or they were who you were five years ago. Fragrance turns. A bottle that has stood open for years smells sharper and flatter than the one you were handed, and one you have not reached for in a full year will not be reached for now. Keep the one you wear and the one you honestly alternate to. The rest go, and the guilt goes with them, because whoever gave it to you wanted you to smell good, not to store glass. The same test sorts the jewellery: worn in the last year stays in the tray, loved but unworn goes to a box in the closet, neither worn nor loved leaves the house.

z.f: Store folded clothing by category
z.i: underwear, socks, sleepwear, shirts, workout clothes
z.s: drawer dividers, vertical folding, labels
z.g: Clothing fits without compression, categories are visible, and drawers open freely
z.c: File-fold vertically so every item is visible from above — stacked folding hides the bottom two-thirds of every drawer.

call.t: The size you are not right now
call.x: Two of these drawers are part filled with clothes that do not fit today, so every morning starts with a small unpleasant reminder instead of a clean choice. Take them out of the bedroom entirely. One box, not two, today's date written on the lid, stored somewhere else in the house. If that box is still sealed a year from now it leaves sealed, and you do not look inside, because looking is how it all comes back. These drawers dress the body you have this morning. That is not giving up on anything. It is refusing to open a drawer and be told off by it every day.

z.f: Store current wardrobe and accessories
z.i: hanging clothes, shoes, bags, belts, seasonal items
z.s: matching hangers, shelf bins, shoe zones, labels
z.g: Current clothing is visible, grouped, reachable, and contained within capacity
z.c: Group by type, then color; one hanger style throughout; and let the reversed-hanger test make the keep/donate calls data-driven.

call.x: There is one thing hanging in here that cost real money and does not fit your life: the suit for the job you left, the coat that is beautiful and far too warm, the shoes that turn on you after twenty minutes. You keep it because letting it go makes the money real. The money is already gone. It left the day you bought it, and keeping the garment does not bring back a penny of it; it just takes a hanger you need and gives you a small flinch every time you slide past. Set one deadline. Photograph it tonight, list it for sale, and if it has not sold in thirty days it goes to the charity shop without another conversation. The lesson is worth keeping. The garment is not.

z.f: Support focused computer and knowledge work
z.i: computer, monitor, keyboard, notebook, phone, current papers
z.s: inbox, action tray, cable clips, device dock
z.g: The desk has a clear work area, current work is contained, and cords are controlled
z.c: The surface standard is current-task tools plus one inbox tray; a reference photo taped nearby makes 'clear' unambiguous.

call.x: One corner of the desk is held by a project you have not touched in weeks and cannot put away, because putting it away feels like admitting it is over. Say the next physical action out loud in one sentence. If you can name it ("call the insurer", "sign page four"), it is live: write that sentence on a card, clip it to the papers, and it goes in the inbox tray, not on the desk. If you cannot name a next action, it is not stalled, it is abandoned. Box it, write today's date on the lid, put it on the shelf, and if the box is still unopened on that date next year, it leaves unopened.

z.f: Store frequently used office tools
z.i: pens, notebooks, stapler, chargers, sticky notes, personal items
z.s: drawer dividers, labels, quantity limits
z.g: Each drawer has one purpose, usable supplies are visible, and duplicates are limited
z.c: Top drawer: daily tools in a tray. Deep drawer: hanging files. Anything unfiled after Friday's inbox-empty is a process escape.

call.x: Somewhere in the pedestal there is a bag or a drawer of cables, adapters, and wall bricks, and it survives because each individual cable is too cheap to think about and too specific to throw away. That decision cannot be made one cable at a time. Empty the whole lot onto the desk at once, pick up each cable, name the device it powers, and point at where that device physically is in this house. No device, no keep. Then keep exactly one spare of each connector type you still use daily, coil and band it, and take the rest to electronics recycling this week. Made in one batch at the cleared desk, it is a single sitting. Made one cable at a time, it never gets made at all.

z.f: Retain and retrieve required documents
z.i: tax records, warranties, household records, project files
z.s: retention labels, folder taxonomy, shred bin
z.g: Files are current, labeled, protected, and easy to retrieve by a simple system
z.c: File by retrieval question ('where would I look?'), purge on a yearly cadence, and scan anything you'd only ever need as information rather than paper.

call.t: What you are actually required to keep
call.x: Most of this drawer is neither obviously permanent nor obviously rubbish, and that middle band is why the whole job stalls. Split it into three by rule. Permanent originals, meaning birth and marriage certificates, deeds, vehicle titles, wills, and immigration papers, go into one closed fireproof box and never into the filing cabinet. Tax returns and their supporting paper get one folder per year and are held for whatever your local retention period is, which you look up once and write on the card. Everything else, the bank statements, the utility bills, the receipts for things you no longer own, goes by this test: if the issuer will reprint it on request, or it already lives inside an online account, it is information, not a record, and information does not get a folder.

z.f: Store reference books and intentional display
z.i: books, binders, manuals, awards, decor
z.s: category labels, bookends, archive limits
z.g: Reference material is grouped and accessible, with stable and uncluttered shelves
z.c: Shelve with 10–15% slack per shelf; a full shelf is a queue with no capacity, and the overflow lands on the nearest flat surface.

call.t: The shelf that says who you used to be
call.x: The textbooks from a degree, the professional library from a job you left, the reference set that a website now answers better and faster. These are the hardest books in the house to release, because they stand for a version of you that you have not formally retired. The rule that settles it: ask when you last took it down since it arrived on this shelf, not whether you might one day. If you cannot name a specific occasion, and the book is one you could borrow or reorder inside a week, it is no longer reference, it is display, and it must now win a display slot in open competition with everything else on the shelf. Most of them will not. Appliance manuals are simpler: model still in the house, keep it; model gone, it goes today.

z.f: Print, scan, and process paper
z.i: printer, scanner, paper, ink, envelopes, cables
z.s: paper bins, ink label, scan tray, cable labels
z.g: Equipment is ready, supplies are stocked to a defined level, and paper flow is clear
z.c: Stage paper and cartridges at point of use with a min/max on the shelf edge; a printer pantry three rooms away is motion waste.

call.x: The old printer is still in the corner, or on the floor of the cupboard, because it might be a backup. Settle it before you leave this corner today: plug it in and print a test page right now. If it prints, and you are prepared to keep a spare cartridge for it in stock, it is a backup and it gets a home. If you will not plug it in today, it is not a backup, it is a large object you have not decided about, and it goes to electronics recycling this week. Apply the same blade to the sealed cartridges: hold each box against the model number on the machine you actually use. Anything unmatched sells this week for more than it will ever be worth again, because cartridge value only falls.

z.f: Store office consumables and backup tools
z.i: paper, pens, tape, folders, labels, envelopes, tech accessories
z.s: clear bins, min-max cards, shelf labels
z.g: Supplies are categorized, counted, and limited to realistic use
z.c: One open of each consumable, backstock behind, min/max labels on the shelf — office supplies obey pantry rules.

call.x: The bulk box of 500 envelopes, the multipack of sticky notes, the case of paper bought because the price was good. The genuinely hard part is that you were not wrong about the price, and admitting the surplus was a mistake feels like throwing money away twice. It is not: the money left when you bought it, and the shelf space is being paid for now. Count the true stock and divide it by your honest annual use, out loud. Six letters a year against 500 envelopes is a lifetime supply and then some. Cap it at one open plus one spare of anything you use monthly, and a single year of use for everything else. The surplus goes to a school, a charity shop, or a neighbour this week. Not to the top shelf, and not to a box in the garage.

z.f: Wash and dry household textiles
z.i: washer, dryer, lint screen, hoses, machine cleaners
z.s: load-status card, lint reminder, machine-clear rule
z.g: Machines are clean, accessible, empty, and ready for the next load
z.c: Lint trap every load, gasket and detergent drawer monthly, hot maintenance wash monthly — machine care is fire prevention wearing chore clothing.

call.t: The duct you have not looked at
call.x: You have been telling yourself the dryer just runs a bit slow these days, and that towels have always needed two cycles. The dryer is not slow, it is blocked. The rule: if you cannot name the month you last pulled the machine out and cleared the duct, that is today's job, no debate. And while the dryer is already out and the duct is disconnected, look at what it is made of. If it is the flexible foil accordion kind, replace it with rigid metal now rather than promising yourself you will do it next time, because there is rarely a next time. Once a year is a cheap habit, and the failure it prevents burns the room it happens in.

z.f: Store laundry chemicals and stain tools
z.i: detergent, bleach, softener, stain remover, measuring tools
z.s: chemical bin, dosing labels, child-safe placement
z.g: Current products are contained, labeled, and stored safely within quantity limits
z.c: Store concentrates on a drip tray at adult height, measured with the cap's actual line — overdosing detergent causes most 'my machine smells' complaints.

call.t: The five half used stain removers
call.x: Every laundry shelf has them: a box of dye grabbing sheets, two spray bottles, a stick that dried solid in the cap, and something a relative swore by. You keep them because binning a mostly full bottle feels wasteful, so instead they sit there being wasteful slowly. The rule: keep the one treatment you have personally watched lift a stain, plus a tub of oxygen powder, which handles most of what the others promise. Everything else leaves today. A treatment you do not trust enough to reach for first is not a supply, it is a decision you have been postponing, and it is holding the one arm's reach of shelf next to the open washer lid.

z.f: Separate dirty laundry by household method
z.i: hampers, baskets, delicates bags, pocket contents
z.s: labeled hampers, pocket tray, fill limits
z.g: Dirty laundry fits within defined categories and the floor remains clear
z.c: Three-way sort at the source (lights, darks, delicates) means any full bag is a machine-ready load with zero re-handling.

call.t: The delicates bag that never fills
call.x: You sort into five streams because a care label once told you to, and one of those bags has been sitting a third full for three weeks while the thing you actually wanted washed waits inside it. The rule: a stream earns its own bag only if it has run as a full load, by itself, in the last month. Everything that fails that test merges into cold and gentle with a mesh bag inside the drum. Sorting is only worth doing when it produces a load you can run today, and a bag that waits three weeks is not sorting, it is a small pile of clothes you have taken out of circulation.

z.f: Fold, pair, and prepare clean laundry for return
z.i: clean laundry, folding board, baskets, hangers
z.s: return baskets, folding boundary, timer cue
z.g: The surface is clear between loads and no clean-laundry backlog remains
z.c: The folding surface carries a same-day rule: what lands folds, what folds returns. It is a workstation, not a shelf.

call.x: You are keeping a growing bag of unmatched socks because tomorrow the partner might surface. Occasionally one does, which is exactly why the bag never gets thrown out, and meanwhile it has become a permanent tenant on the one surface in this room that has to stay clear. The rule: singles get one shoebox and nothing larger. When the box is full, or at the change of season, whichever arrives first, everything still unmatched becomes a cleaning rag or leaves the house. A sock that has waited a whole season is not going to be reunited. It is just going to keep charging you the counter, and the counter is where the whole room jams.

z.f: Dry items that should not enter the dryer
z.i: drying rack, hangers, delicates, drip-dry items
z.s: hanger limit, drip tray, dry-date tag
z.g: Air-dry items fit without crowding and are removed promptly when dry
z.c: Cap the rod: when hanging space is full, the oldest items move on — a full rod is a queue pretending to be storage.

call.t: The garment that only ever hangs
call.x: There is at least one thing on that rack you have washed more times than you have worn. It is hand wash only, it takes two days to give up its water, and it holds the rack hostage the entire time while everything else waits its turn. The rule: think back to the last three times it was washed and name the occasion you wore it for each one. If you cannot name all three, the garment is charging you rack space and drying days it has not earned, and it goes. Line dry only is a real running cost, not a neutral care label, and it should only ever be paid for clothes you genuinely reach for.

z.f: Store tools used to maintain the laundry area
z.i: broom, mop, vacuum attachments, rags, trash bags
z.s: wall hooks, labeled caddy, floor boundary
z.g: Cleaning tools are secure, dry, and easy to retrieve without blocking machines
z.c: Hang tools handle-up on a rail — bristles and heads that touch the floor deform and re-soil; nothing stores wet.

call.x: Worn towels, holed T-shirts and a retired set of sheets have quietly become a rag supply large enough to clean a small hotel. It grows because turning a worn item into a rag feels like thrift rather than a decision, so nothing is ever really discarded, only reclassified. The rule: rags live in one bin and only one bin, and nothing new becomes a rag until something old leaves as waste. If you cannot work through one bin of rags in a year, you are not saving cloth, you are storing it in the room with the least spare space. The same rule settles the second vacuum you are keeping for the garage: if it has not run in a year, it is not a spare, it is a broken machine with an excuse.
